docs.title: Chora
docs.text:
Chora is the space where forms appear.

Chora is a Wayland compositor without policy. It is a programmable scene, not a desktop.

Chora has no window manager, no layout, no keybindings and no look. The core renders a small scene of primitives and offers one API. Plugins add all other behavior. A plugin can supply a stacking desktop, a tiling workflow, or a view that an agent arranges live by voice. Only a small safety layer is built in.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Concept phase. The repository holds the design documents. There is no code yet.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text: Every part of Chora gets a check against existing projects. This page records the first check from October 2026. An entry with the mark unverified needs a second look.

docs.title: Compositors
docs.text:
Project Stack Extension model Fit for Chora Missing River 0.4 Zig, wlroots the window manager is a separate process; it speaks the stable river-window-management-v1 protocol with atomic, frame-perfect updates closest to "the window manager is a plugin" no scene graph, no shaders or effects Pinnacle Rust, Smithay gRPC API with Lua and Rust clients; Snowcap widgets best Rust base for a fork: the policy already lives outside the compositor no scene primitives, no shader nodes, no MCP; small team niri Rust, Smithay KDL config, niri msg IPC, no plugins best Smithay reference for rendering, shaders, blur and animations scrolling tiling is built in cosmic-comp Rust, Smithay none production-grade Smithay reference bound to COSMIC Jay Rust, own stack config as a Rust library (unverified) reference for a Vulkan renderer not Smithay; GPLv3 Wayfire C++, wlroots in-process C++ plugins, IPC close plugin idea, 3D effects unsafe C++ ABI, slow releases Hyprland C++, Aquamarine C++ plugins with an unstable ABI, Lua config the target effects opinionated; the plugin ABI breaks with every release Mir and MirAL C++ libraries for shells mature C++; the policy model of MirAL Louvre C++ library with defaults that can be replaced good scene API not Rust scenefx C, wlroots wlroots scene with blur, shadows and rounded corners scene graph and effects C and wlroots only CwC, SomeWM, Strata C and Lua, Rust and Lua scripted configs scriptable no policy-free core with a scene graph

Agent tools exist today only as external MCP servers on top of existing compositors, for example kwin-mcp, and hypruse for Hyprland. The check found no compositor with WASM plugins or built-in MCP. The combination of Chora appears to be new: a policy-free core, a scene of primitives with shaders, and one API for plugins, IPC and MCP.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. Build on Smithay and copy from others. Sources: the anvil and smallvil examples, niri, cosmic-comp, Pinnacle. This option gives full control of the scene and the plugin model. This is the decision (D14).
  2. Fork Pinnacle. A working Smithay compositor with an external API on day one. The code review below rejects this option.
  3. River 0.4 with a Rust window manager. No compositor code, but no shaders, no effects and no scene. This option drops the game-engine half of the idea. It is a fallback for a quick tiling prototype.
  4. An MCP server on an existing compositor, like kwin-mcp. This is the fastest way to try agentic workflows. It gives no canvas and no effects.

River shows a strong design for the window manager interface. Chora can copy its semantics without its code.

docs.title: Pinnacle code review
docs.text:
The review measured a clone of Pinnacle 0.2.2 (last commit 2026-06-27).

  • Size: 34,138 lines of Rust in src/. The workspace adds the client API (Rust and Lua), the Snowcap widget toolkit and a wlcs test adapter.
  • Policy in the core: tags touch 20 files, layout modes 20 files, window rules 8 files. Click-to-focus is hardcoded.
  • Rendering: a flat list of Smithay render elements on top of Smithay's Space. No scene graph and no custom shaders. Space appears in 23 files.
  • API: tonic gRPC with 115 methods around tags and layout modes. No batching and no transactions for clients.
  • Transactions: yes, for window positions per output. A transaction completes when every window commits, or after 150 ms. The design comes from niri.
  • License: GPL-3.0-or-later. src/protocol/drm.rs is GPL-3.0-only. The API crates and Snowcap are MPL-2.0.
  • Activity: 57 commits in February 2026, then 2, 3 and 8 per month.

A fork keeps about 40 to 50 percent of src/. It deletes or rewrites the spine that Chora replaces: Space, the window state, tags and the API. Only the generic parts survive, and these are easy to copy. Dependencies lists them.

docs.title: Plugin runtimes
docs.text:
Runtime Strengths Weaknesses Extism on wasmtime more than 13 guest languages, simple, sandboxed bytes in, bytes out: every call serializes and copies wasmtime with the Component Model typed WIT interfaces, handles to scene nodes, fuel and epoch limits, fast new instances fewer mature guest languages; Rust is first-class wasmer works less momentum for the Component Model mlua with LuaJIT or Luau low friction, easy reload, Luau sandbox no memory isolation from the host Rhai pure Rust, easy slow tree-walking interpreter Rune native to Rust not at 1.0 deno_core (V8) JS and TS ecosystem heavy, GC pauses, API churn abi_stable dylibs native speed stale, unsafe unloading, no sandbox IPC clients (separate processes) any language, crash isolation from the OS, no runtime in the core a round trip per event; no code in every frame

For code in every frame, the Component Model is better than Extism. Typed calls only help when the boundary stays typed: JSON over WIT gives back the cost of Extism. Chora starts with IPC clients only (D27). wasmtime comes when a measurement demands it.

docs.title: Renderer
docs.text:
• niri, cosmic-comp and Pinnacle use the GLES renderer of Smithay. Custom GLSL shaders through texture and pixel shader elements work in practice, for example the blur of niri.
  • No Smithay compositor renders through wgpu. The Smithay maintainers consider wgpu too abstract for a compositor. Smithay has no merged Vulkan renderer either.
  • Decision: GLES and GLSL (D16).

docs.title: MCP
docs.text: rmcp 3.x supports stdio and Streamable HTTP. choractl mcp uses stdio. A container gets the socket through a bind mount, so Chora needs no network transport for now.

docs.title: Widgets and shells
docs.text:
Quickshell is the strongest choice: Qt6 and QML, declarative, with live reload. waybar is mature. eww and AGS/Astal need a check of their activity. All of these need wlr-layer-shell.

For HTML from agents, a browser in app mode (chromium --app=...) is enough (D35). Chora places toplevels anywhere. A dedicated host on gtk4-layer-shell with WebKitGTK, or a Tauri window as a layer surface, is an option for later.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Draft

A first sketch of the one API of Chora. Names and shapes will change. The principle stays: plugins, IPC clients and agents use one language of commands and events.

docs.title: Model
docs.text:
A command changes the scene. An event reports a change. Commands travel in transactions (see Architecture).

# one transaction
- create: {id: work, kind: group, parent: root}
- create: {id: bg, kind: shader, parent: work, shader: aurora.frag}
- attach: {surface: s42, parent: work}
- configure: {surface: s42, size: [900, 600], states: [activated]}
- update: {id: s42, transform: {translate: [40, 40, 0]}}
- update: {id: work, effects: [{shader: blur.frag, uniforms: {radius: 8}}]}
- focus: {surface: s42}

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
This table is the one list of node properties.

Property Nodes Meaning id all stable id; the core assigns ids to surfaces owner all the client that created or attached the node; read-only transform all a 4x4 matrix, or the short form translate, scale, rotate opacity, visible all clip all rectangle, optionally rounded effects all list of shaders with uniforms input all accept, pass or block meta all free key/value pairs to tag and find nodes size rect, shader width and height color, radius, border rect shader, uniforms shader GLSL ES file and its inputs; a uniform can name another node as a texture

A surface node gets its size from its client. The configure command asks the client for a new size.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Command Purpose create create a group, rect or shader node under a parent attach put a detached surface node under a parent update change node properties animate change properties over a duration with an easing curve move change the parent or the position among the siblings remove remove a node; a removed surface becomes detached configure send size, toplevel states (activated, tiled, maximized, fullscreen) and decoration mode to a client focus set the keyboard focus close ask a client to close a surface viewport set the viewport of an output: a transform from scene coordinates to output pixels

Only the owner of a node can change it. animate lets plugins and agents animate without code in every frame.

docs.title: Selectors
docs.text: A selector finds nodes without an id: id:work, app_id:firefox, title~:Inbox, meta:role=editor, kind:surface. Selectors work in queries only. A query returns all current matches, or an empty list. It always sees the current titles.

docs.title: Events
docs.text: Event Data surface.created, surface.destroyed surface id, app_id, title, role (toplevel, layer, popup) surface.changed title, app_id, min and max size, requests for maximize, fullscreen and activation input.key, input.pointer, input.touch, input.gesture event data for grabs output.added, output.removed, output.changed output, mode, scale plugin.connected, plugin.disconnected name, reason transaction.applied, transaction.rejected id, error, for example a shader compile error

docs.title: IPC methods
docs.text:
JSON-RPC 2.0 on the socket in CHORA_SOCKET.

Method Purpose scene.query(selector) read nodes scene.apply(transaction) apply a transaction events.subscribe(filter) stream events input.grab(binding) get the events of a key, a button or a gesture input.inject(events) send synthetic input; needs approval screen.capture(target) capture an output, a group or a surface; needs approval output.list list the outputs and their viewports methods.export(names) offer methods of this plugin to other clients methods.call(plugin, method, params) call a method of a plugin

The core implements wlr-output-management, so kanshi and wlr-randr configure the outputs. The API has no output configuration of its own.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
A plugin is an IPC client with a manifest:

name: tiling
exec: chora-tiling
subscribe: [surface.created, surface.destroyed, output.changed]
grabs: [Super+h, Super+l]
methods: [set_layout, resize]

A plugin owns the nodes that it creates. The core removes them when the plugin disconnects.

docs.title: MCP tools
docs.text: choractl mcp offers the IPC methods as MCP tools. It also offers tools for whole tasks, for example "describe the screen", which returns a screenshot and the scene tree. The agent then sees the result of its changes.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Draft

This page follows the Decisions. The first implementation will refine it.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph core["chora (Rust, Smithay)"]
        protocols["Wayland protocols"]
        backends["Backends: DRM/KMS and libinput, winit for development"]
        scene["Scene: group, surface, rect, shader"]
        render["Renderer: GLES and GLSL shaders"]
        input["Input router"]
        ipc["IPC socket: JSON-RPC"]
        safety["Safety layer"]
    end
    clients["Wayland clients: apps, Quickshell, waybar, browsers"] <--> protocols
    plugins["Plugins: WM, layouts, keybindings"] <--> ipc
    choractl["choractl: CLI and MCP bridge"] <--> ipc
    services["Services in containers"] <--> ipc
    agents["Agents: MCP clients"] <--> choractl
    services -.-> clients
    plugins -.-> clients

The core has one language: commands and events (see API). Plugins, choractl, services and agents all use it. Nothing outside the core changes the scene in another way.

Plugins are separate processes (D27). A plugin can also be a Wayland client, for example to draw window decorations as its own surfaces.

docs.title: Core
docs.text:
The compositor binary chora. Its tasks, and nothing more:

  • Wayland protocol handling and the client lifecycle, through Smithay.
  • Backends: DRM/KMS and libinput on real hardware, through libseat. A winit window for development inside another compositor.
  • The scene, rendered every frame.
  • Input routing (see below).
  • The IPC socket.
  • The safety layer (see below).

The core places popups, subsurfaces and layer surfaces itself, because the protocols define their position. Smithay's PopupManager and LayerMap do this work. Only toplevels wait for a plugin: the core creates a detached surface node and sends surface.created. A plugin decides where the surface appears, or if it appears at all.

docs.title: Scene
docs.text:
The scene is a tree of nodes with stable ids. API lists the node properties. The order of the children sets the stacking order. The crate chora-scene holds the scene model (see Project structure).

All outputs show one logical scene. Each output has a viewport: a transform from scene coordinates to output pixels. A plugin moves or scales a viewport to pan or zoom. Two outputs side by side get two adjacent viewports. One window across two outputs then needs no special case.

Each node has one owner: the client that created or attached it. The core rejects changes from other clients. When a plugin disconnects, the core removes its nodes. Its surfaces become detached.

docs.title: Renderer
docs.text:
The core uses Smithay's GLES renderer through Smithay's own renderer traits. Custom texture and pixel shaders give blur, rounded corners, shadows, color effects and transitions. niri shows what this approach can do. Shaders are GLSL ES. The core compiles them at runtime and reloads them when they change. A shader can read other nodes as textures.

Transforms are 4x4 matrices, so 3D effects need no API change. The first milestone renders and tests 2D cases only.

Damage tracking keeps the GPU load low. Each shader declares if it is static or animated, and effects expand the damage area. A fullscreen surface without effects goes to direct scanout.

docs.title: IPC socket
docs.text:
JSON-RPC 2.0 on a Unix socket. The core exports its path as CHORA_SOCKET. choractl, plugins and services connect to it. Event subscriptions stream over the same connection.

A plugin can export methods, for example tiling.set_layout. The core forwards a method call to the plugin and returns the answer. An agent then asks the window manager for a change instead of fighting it.

docs.title: choractl and the MCP bridge
docs.text: choractl is the CLI for the coordinator. It loads views and starts their plugins. choractl mcp serves the API as MCP tools over stdio. MCP stays out of the core, so the MCP side can change without a change to the compositor.

docs.title: Transactions
docs.text:
A transaction is a batch of commands. The core applies it as one unit.

Some commands need a client round trip. A resize sends a configure event, and the client must answer with a new buffer. The core therefore holds the transaction until all affected clients commit, or until a deadline passes. Then the core shows all changes in the same frame. Sway, niri, River and Pinnacle work the same way.

docs.title: Frame flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Backend
    participant C as Core
    participant R as Renderer
    B->>C: vblank
    C->>C: apply the transactions that are ready
    C->>C: advance the running animations
    C->>R: render the damaged parts of each viewport
    R-->>B: page flip

docs.title: Input flow
docs.text:
1. libinput sends an event to the core.
  2. The safety layer checks its fixed bindings first.
  3. The plugins that grabbed the key or the pointer get the event. A plugin consumes the event or lets it pass.
  4. The focused surface gets each event that no plugin consumed. Pointer events go to the topmost node under the cursor that accepts input.

Focus is state in the scene, and plugins set it. The core never sets focus by itself. The core still implements the protocol mechanisms around focus: popup grabs, xdg-activation requests, pointer-constraints and input-method.

docs.title: Safety layer
docs.text:
The safety layer is the only built-in behavior (see Vision). No plugin and no IPC client can change it.

  • Fixed bindings for VT switch, quit and emergency reset. Injected input never triggers them.
  • Emergency reset. The core disconnects all plugins, removes all effects and puts all surfaces in a simple grid. This grid is the one layout in the core. It is hardcoded, so a broken configuration cannot break it.
  • Session lock. The core enforces ext-session-lock. The lock surface is above every plugin node.
  • Watchdog. When frames miss their deadline repeatedly, the core removes the effects first and then disconnects the plugins.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Version 1 trusts every client of the same user on the IPC socket, as sway does. Three mechanisms add protection:

  • wp-security-context-v1 hides privileged Wayland protocols, for example screencopy and virtual keyboards, from sandboxed clients.
  • A container gets a restricted IPC socket through a bind mount.
  • Input injection and screen capture need the approval of the user.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
• A binary and a chora.desktop session file. A display manager then offers Chora next to the existing desktops.
  • A derived secureblue image, built with secureblue-images and image-builder-action, installs Chora.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Views are YAML files in git, and an agent can read and write them. A strict schema validates each file. It rejects unknown keys and catches the YAML traps, for example no read as false.

The core reads no configuration file. It starts one command, usually the systemd target of a flavor:

chora -- systemctl --user start tiling.target

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
~/.config/chora/
├── views/      # one file per view
├── flavors/    # bundles of views, plugins and services
├── plugins/    # plugin manifests
└── shaders/    # GLSL ES shaders

The directory is a git repository. It contains no secrets.

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
A view is a part of the scene and the plugins that drive it. choractl view load <name> starts the plugins of the view and applies its nodes as one transaction. Only choractl starts plugins.

# ~/.config/chora/views/analysis.yaml
name: analysis
plugins:
- name: tiling
  config: {layout: columns, gap: 12}
- name: keybindings
  config:
    bindings:
      Super+Return: {spawn: wezterm}
      Super+q: close
scene:
- id: workspace
  kind: group
  effects: [{shader: vignette.frag, uniforms: {strength: 0.3}}]

The tiling plugin places the surfaces in workspace. The view only names the plugin and its configuration.

docs.title: Flavors
docs.text:
A flavor is a directory with views, plugin manifests and services, plus a systemd user target. The target starts the services and then loads the first view with choractl. systemd handles start, restart and order, so Chora needs no service manager.

flavors/agentic/
├── agentic.target
├── views/       # morning, analysis, writing, coding
├── plugins/     # canvas layout, keybindings
└── services/    # Quadlet units: speech, browser in app mode

docs.title: Services
docs.text: A service runs as a Quadlet unit with Podman, or in distrobox. It connects to the IPC socket, appears as a Wayland client, or both. A container gets the IPC socket through a bind mount.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text: The decision log. Nothing here is final. Every entry can come back for review.

docs.title: Principles and scope
docs.text: # Decision Reason D1 Rust and Smithay for the core Smithay is a library without policy, proven in niri and cosmic-comp. Rust is safe when agents change the system live. D2 Everything is a plugin Maximum flexibility and a small core. D3 An experimentation platform first, then a stable, feature-complete core, then testing A small core gives stability. D4 Reuse before writing; check alternatives for every decision Little code to maintain. D5 One vocabulary, defined in the Glossary One language for people and agents. D6 Inventory and agent memory form a separate layer, not part of the core The platform stays neutral. D7 The name is Chora Plato's χώρα is the space that gives forms a place. It has no form of its own. D8 The core is GPL-3.0-or-later The core can then reuse code from Pinnacle and niri. Code under GPL-3.0-only stays out. D9 English for code and documentation The documentation is public.

docs.title: Platform
docs.text: # Decision Reason D10 Fedora and secureblue as host; a derived image offers Chora as an additional session The system and the image tooling of the author. D11 AMD and Intel GPUs first, NVIDIA later The hardware of the author. Mesa drivers need no special paths. D12 Services run as Quadlet units with Podman or in distrobox; a container gets the IPC socket through a bind mount Isolation. systemd handles start, restart and order. D13 The coordinator is the user first, later an agent with special permissions A gradual path to control by agents.

docs.title: Core
docs.text: # Decision Reason D14 Build on Smithay; copy from Pinnacle, niri and anvil; no fork A fork of Pinnacle keeps less than half of its code. Its spine (Space, tags, the gRPC API) is what Chora replaces. See Alternatives. D15 Pin a Smithay git revision No Smithay release since 0.7.0. All major users track git. D16 GLES renderer and GLSL shaders through Smithay's renderer traits Proven in niri. No Smithay compositor uses wgpu. D17 Four node kinds: group, surface, rect, shader Text, images and widgets come from Wayland clients. A shader can read another node as a texture. D18 Transforms are 4x4 matrices; the first milestone tests 2D cases only 3D effects need no API change later. D19 One logical scene; each output shows it through a viewport Pan, zoom and the infinite canvas need no extra mechanism. D20 The core places popups, subsurfaces and layer surfaces; toplevels wait for a plugin The protocols define these positions. Smithay implements them. D21 A transaction completes when all affected clients commit, or after a deadline A resize needs a client round trip. Sway, niri, River and Pinnacle do the same. D22 A hardcoded safety layer A recovery path must not depend on a file that an agent can break. D23 Shaders declare static or animated; fullscreen surfaces without effects use direct scanout Damage tracking and battery life. D24 No undo history and no plugin state store in the core A destroyed client cannot come back. The reset and the views in git cover recovery. The scene holds all state. D25 Xwayland through xwayland-satellite Keeps the core small. D26 Output configuration through wlr-output-management kanshi and wlr-randr exist.

docs.title: Plugins and API
docs.text: # Decision Reason D27 Plugins are IPC clients; the core offers animate; in-process WASM plugins come only after a measurement shows the need Agents work in seconds, not frames. One mechanism, any language, crash isolation by the OS. D28 Each node has one owner; plugins export methods An agent asks the window manager instead of fighting it. D29 Selectors work in queries only; a query returns all current matches No window rules in the core. Predictable results for agents. D30 Version 1 trusts the clients of the same user; wp-security-context-v1 hides privileged protocols from sandboxed clients; input injection and screen capture need the approval of the user Little code first, still safe for containers. D31 MCP outside the core: choractl mcp over stdio, with tools for whole tasks The core stays free of MCP. D32 The core reads no configuration; choractl loads YAML views; a flavor is a directory with a systemd target; the configuration holds no secrets Policy and service management do not belong in the core. D33 Three crates to start: chora-scene, chora, choractl A crate comes when a second consumer needs it.

docs.title: Tools around the core
docs.text: # Decision Reason D34 Screen sharing through xdg-desktop-portal-wlr first No code. A portal backend of its own is in the Idea backlog. D35 HTML content from agents runs in a browser in app mode, as a service No code. Chora places toplevels anywhere.

docs.title: Rejected review findings
docs.text: Finding Reason Versioned docs with mike are too much The project conventions use mike. Hooks without matching files The project conventions use this hook set in every repository. Cargo hooks before the first crate Requested from the start. They stay inactive until the first Rust file.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
1. Approval. How does the user approve input injection and screen capture? A dialog that the safety layer draws, or a prompt in choractl?
  2. YAML crate. Which maintained crate replaces serde_yaml?
  3. Repository name. The GitHub repository still has the name void.

docs.text: The parts that Chora reuses. Alternatives records the check of each choice. Decisions records the result.

docs.text: Dependency Purpose Notes a maintained YAML crate views serde_yaml is unmaintained rmcp choractl mcp the official Rust MCP SDK, version 3.x

docs.title: Code to copy
docs.text:
The core is GPL-3.0-or-later, so it can reuse GPL code. Code under GPL-3.0-only stays out, for example src/protocol/drm.rs of Pinnacle.

Source Parts Pinnacle transactions (util/transaction.rs, hook.rs), wlr protocol implementations (protocol/), udev and winit backends, the handoff from the IPC thread to the event loop (api.rs), the wlcs test adapter niri custom shaders, blur, offscreen rendering, animations anvil and smallvil (Smithay) minimal compositor structure

docs.title: Wayland protocols
docs.text:
The core speaks these protocols, so existing tools work unchanged:

  • Base: xdg-shell, xdg-decoration, viewporter, fractional-scale, linux-dmabuf, presentation-time, xdg-output, cursor-shape, data device, primary-selection.
  • Shells and widgets: wlr-layer-shell, ext-foreign-toplevel-list, wlr-foreign-toplevel-management, xdg-activation.
  • Desktop integration: ext-session-lock, ext-idle-notify, idle-inhibit, text-input, input-method, pointer-constraints, relative-pointer, wlr-output-management.
  • Capture: ext-image-copy-capture and wlr-screencopy.
  • Isolation: wp-security-context-v1.

docs.title: Outside the core
docs.text: Tool Role xwayland-satellite Xwayland as a separate process xdg-desktop-portal-wlr screen sharing Quickshell, waybar, eww, AGS/Astal bars, panels, widgets fuzzel, wofi launchers swaybg, swww wallpapers Chromium or Firefox in app mode HTML content from agents whisper.cpp or faster-whisper, piper speech in and out Podman with Quadlet, distrobox, systemd user units services and flavors kanshi, wlr-randr output configuration

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The shared vocabulary of Chora. Code, docs and prompts to agents use these terms and no synonyms.

Term Meaning Core The compositor process chora. It handles the Wayland protocols, the backends (DRM/KMS, libinput), the scene, the renderer, the input routing, the IPC socket and the safety layer. It contains no policy. Scene The tree of nodes that the core renders every frame. It is the single source of truth for the screen content. Node One element of the scene. The kinds are group, surface, rect and shader. Every node has an id, an owner, a transform, an opacity and optional effects. Group A node that contains other nodes. It applies a transform, a clip, an opacity and optional effects to its children. Canvas A group that serves as a working area: a workspace, a desktop or an infinite zoomable plane. Surface A node that shows a Wayland client: an application window, a layer-shell widget or a browser window. For the core, a surface is a texture source and an input target. Rect A colored rectangle with optional rounded corners and border. Shader A node that a fragment shader draws completely. A shader can read other nodes as textures. A shader can also be an effect. Effect A shader that changes how a node and its children look, for example blur or a color change. Every node can have effects. Viewport The part of the scene that one output shows. A viewport is a transform from scene coordinates to output pixels. Owner The client that created or attached a node. Only the owner changes the node. Toplevel A surface with the role of an application window (xdg_toplevel). Other roles are layer surfaces and popups. Detached The state of a surface node without a parent. A detached surface is not visible. View A declarative arrangement: nodes, the plugins that drive them, and their configuration. A view is a YAML file in git. The user or an agent changes it live. Plugin A process that reacts to events, changes the scene through the IPC socket and can export methods. A window manager, a layout, an animation set and a keybinding set are plugins. Service A process in a container, outside the core. Examples are speech recognition, a local LLM and a development environment. Configuration shows how services run. Flavor A preconfigured bundle of views, plugins and services, for example "classic", "tiling" or "agentic". Coordinator The party that installs and connects plugins, services and flavors. First the user, later an agent with special permissions. Inventory A local, git-versioned store of reusable elements (views, plugins, widgets). It belongs to the opinionated layer above Chora, not to the core. Command A request to change the scene, for example create or update. Event A message from the core about a change, for example surface.created. Selector An expression that finds nodes without an id, for example app_id:firefox. Transaction A batch of commands that the core applies as one unit. If one command fails, the core applies none of them. Safety layer The only built-in behavior of the core: fixed bindings, emergency reset, session lock, watchdog.

docs.title: Idea backlog
docs.text: All ideas that are not decisions yet. An idea moves to Decisions or leaves the list.

docs.title: Interaction
docs.text:
• Voice as the main channel to an agent: speech to text in, text to speech out, with a robust push-to-talk or wake-word mechanism.
  • A morning view: greeting, current tasks, sorted email, and a day plan that user and agent prioritize together.
  • A view for each task, built on demand: data analysis with data, plots and interactive exploration; email; web research; coding.
  • Live changes by voice: resize, rearrange, highlight, dim, switch views.
  • Views that fit the task and the taste of the user. The agent learns the layout preferences of the user.

docs.title: Visuals
docs.text:
• Effects like in Hyprland and Compiz: blur, shadows, rounded corners, wobbly windows, cube, overview, transitions.
  • An infinite zoomable canvas through viewports.
  • Surfaces as 3D objects.
  • Pixel-perfect copies of existing desktops (Windows XP, KDE Plasma) as flavors. They prove the flexibility. They are not a goal.

docs.title: Agents and the ecosystem around Chora
docs.text:
• An inventory: a local, git-versioned store of reusable elements. Code for one-time use goes away, useful code stays.
  • Agent memory in the home directory.
  • Demiurge as the name of the coordinating agent. In Plato, the demiurge shapes the forms in the chora.

docs.title: Core extensions
docs.text:
• In-process WASM plugins on wasmtime with the Component Model, for effects that need code in every frame, for example wobbly windows. Only after a measurement shows the need (D27).
  • A portal backend of its own, so that screen sharing can share a group or a canvas instead of a whole output or window.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
• A local inference engine (LLM) in a container.
  • Speech services (whisper, piper).
  • Development environments with special configurations (distrobox).
  • A dedicated webview host on gtk4-layer-shell, if a browser in app mode is too slow, too heavy or cannot be transparent.

docs.title: Platform
docs.text:
• Flavors as installable bundles: classic, tiling, agentic.
  • A later registry for plugins and flavors, possibly as OCI artifacts. OCI fits the container world of the host.

docs.title: Project structure
docs.text:
The planned layout of this repository: one Cargo workspace with as few crates as possible. A module moves into its own crate only when a second consumer needs it. No crate exists yet.

chora/
├── crates/
│   ├── chora-scene/   # scene model, commands, events, transactions, selectors; no Smithay
│   ├── chora/         # the compositor: Smithay, backends, renderer, input, safety, IPC
│   └── choractl/      # CLI over the IPC socket; `choractl mcp` is the MCP bridge
├── plugins/           # reference plugins: tiling, stacking, keybindings
├── dist/              # chora.desktop session file, packaging
├── docs/              # this documentation (MkDocs)
├── mkdocs.yml
└── Cargo.toml         # workspace, lints

docs.title: Reasons for this split
docs.text:
• chora-scene has no Smithay dependency. Tests of the data model and the transaction logic need no GPU and no compositor. The core, choractl and plugins share this one definition of the API.
  • Reference plugins live in this repository first. They keep the API honest. They can move out when the API is stable.
  • The build generates the schemas from the Rust types. The repository does not contain them. Docs, validation and agents then see the same contract.

docs.title: Related repositories
docs.text: Repository Role secureblue-images derived image that installs Chora as an additional session image-builder-action builds and signs that image distrobox-images container images for services

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
Draft

A first proposal. The order and the scope of the milestones are open for discussion.

Each milestone has a goal, a scope and an exit criterion. A milestone is done when its exit criterion holds on the real setup of the author. After M6 the core is feature complete, and testing starts (D3).

docs.title: M0: Workspace and tooling
docs.text:
Goal: the first line of Rust already meets all guards.

  • Cargo workspace with chora-scene, chora and choractl (D33).
  • Workspace lints: clippy pedantic, cognitive_complexity, excessive_nesting; unsafe_code denied. clippy.toml sets the limits.
  • A CI workflow for cargo test, and cargo-deny for licenses and advisories. The license check keeps GPL-3.0-only code out (D8).
  • Dependabot for Cargo. A pinned Smithay revision (D15).

Exit: CI is green. chora opens an empty winit window.

docs.title: M1: Nested proof of concept
docs.text:
Goal: the smallest proof of the concept, inside an existing session.

  • winit backend, xdg-shell toplevels and popups.
  • Scene with group, surface and rect nodes, 2D transforms (D17, D18).
  • Transactions that wait for client commits (D21).
  • IPC socket with scene.query, scene.apply, events.subscribe and input.grab.
  • Safety layer: quit and emergency reset (D22).
  • choractl with basic commands.
  • A tiling plugin as IPC client, as reference.

Exit: the tiling plugin arranges terminal windows in the nested session. A crash of the plugin leaves the core running. The reset works.

docs.title: M2: Session on real hardware
docs.text:
Goal: Chora runs as a login session on AMD and Intel (D11).

  • udev, DRM/KMS, libinput and libseat backends, copied from Pinnacle.
  • Several outputs with viewports (D19), wlr-output-management (D26).
  • wlr-layer-shell, so waybar, fuzzel and Quickshell work.
  • ext-session-lock, idle protocols, xwayland-satellite (D25).
  • chora.desktop session file.

Exit: a tiling session with bar and launcher runs for a full workday.

docs.title: M3: Agent interface
docs.text:
Goal: an agent sees and changes the screen.

  • choractl mcp over stdio, with tools for whole tasks (D31).
  • screen.capture and input.inject, both with approval (D30).
  • Node ownership and plugin methods (D28).
  • choractl loads and saves YAML views (D32).
  • wp-security-context-v1.

Exit: an agent rearranges views over MCP and checks the result with screenshots.

docs.title: M4: Effects
docs.text:
Goal: the game-engine half of the idea.

  • Shader nodes, effects and shaders that read nodes as textures (D17).
  • GLSL hot reload; compile errors as transaction.rejected.
  • The animate command (D27).
  • Damage tracking for static and animated shaders, direct scanout (D23).
  • The watchdog of the safety layer.

Exit: blur, rounded corners and animated transitions run at the full frame rate of the output.

docs.title: M5: Packaging
docs.text:
Goal: Chora installs like every other desktop on the host.

  • A derived secureblue image with the Chora session (D10).
  • Flavors as directories with systemd targets: tiling first (D32).
  • Services as Quadlet units (D12).

Exit: after an image update, the login screen offers Chora.

docs.title: M6: Agentic flavor
docs.text:
Goal: the agentic workday scenario works end to end.

  • Speech services: whisper.cpp or faster-whisper, piper.
  • A browser in app mode as service for HTML content (D35).
  • Morning view and task views.

Exit: the user plans the day by voice, and the agent builds the views for the tasks.

docs.title: After M6
docs.text:
• Conformance tests with wlcs, as Pinnacle does.
  • Hardening and testing on the daily system.
  • Items from the Idea backlog, for example in-process WASM plugins or a portal backend of its own.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text: Three scenarios test the concept and estimate the effort on top of the core. The estimates are rough. They assume that the core implements the common Wayland protocols (see Dependencies), so existing tools work unchanged.

docs.title: 1. Classic desktop
docs.text:
A Windows-like desktop with taskbar, start menu and overlapping windows, driven by mouse and keyboard. This is not the goal of Chora, but it must be possible.

Part Source Effort Stacking window manager: move, resize, raise, focus, minimize plugin about 1000 to 2000 lines Window decorations: title bar, buttons plugin with rect and shader nodes, a decoration surface of the plugin, or client-side decorations small to medium Keybindings: Alt+Tab, Super key plugin small Taskbar, tray, clock existing shell: Quickshell, waybar, eww configuration Start menu, launcher fuzzel, wofi or a Quickshell widget configuration Wallpaper swaybg or swww configuration Pixel-perfect XP look theme assets, shaders, decorations much detail work, little difficulty

The taskbar needs the foreign-toplevel protocols to see the windows. The launcher and the bar need wlr-layer-shell.

Result: medium effort, almost all of it in one window manager plugin.

docs.title: 2. Keyboard-driven tiling
docs.text:
A Linux-style tiling workflow with workspaces. The user configures it.

Part Source Effort Tiling layout: master and stack, columns, scrolling plugin a few hundred lines Workspaces one group per workspace, switched by visibility or transform small Keybindings, focus movement plugin small Bar waybar or Quickshell configuration Animations the animate command of the core small

Result: low effort. This is a good first flavor to test the plugin API.

docs.title: 3. Agentic workday
docs.text:
This scenario is the core idea. A robust voice channel connects the user to an agent, and the agent arranges content for each task.

  1. Morning view. The agent greets the user and shows the current tasks. It sorts the email. User and agent plan and prioritize the day together.
  2. Task views. The agent builds a new canvas for each task and fills it. A data analysis gets prepared data, plots and interactive exploration. Email, web research and coding get their own views.
  3. Reuse. The inventory keeps useful elements in git for later use. The agent discards code for one-time use.
  4. Live change by voice. "Make the plot bigger." "Put the terminal next to the notebook." "Dim everything except the editor." The agent calls the methods of the window manager plugin for these changes.
Part Source Effort Scene access for the agent IPC socket and choractl mcp part of the API Speech in and out services: whisper.cpp or faster-whisper, piper integration The agent Claude Code or another MCP client, later a local LLM service integration Rich content: greeting, plots, email the agent writes HTML, a browser in app mode shows it as a surface generated content Data exploration Jupyter, marimo or a plot web app as surfaces existing tools One view per task YAML views that choractl loads, saves and changes live coordinator tool Inventory, memory opinionated layer above Chora later

Result: the largest scenario, but mostly integration of existing parts. The core must supply scene queries and changes, screenshots and input injection. Input injection and screen capture need the approval of the user. The agent needs screenshots to see the result of its changes.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
• The four node kinds cover all three scenarios.
  • Text, images and widgets do not need to live in the core. Existing shells, wallpaper tools and a browser in app mode supply them.
  • Two core features decide the success. The protocol coverage lets existing tools work. The API lets plugins and agents arrange everything.

docs.title: Vision and principles
docs.text: Chora is the space where forms appear.

docs.title: The name
docs.text: Plato calls the space in which things come into being chora (χώρα). Chora is neither form nor matter. It only gives the forms a place. The compositor works the same way: it has no content and no policy of its own. Plugins, clients and agents bring the forms.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
A desktop decides the arrangement of the content: windows, panels, workspaces. Chora takes this decision out of the compositor. Chora is a programmable scene. It works more like a game engine than like a window manager. The core renders a scene of nodes every frame. One API changes the scene live.

The motivating use case is agentic interaction. The user talks to an agent, ideally by voice. The agent arranges the screen for the current task and for the taste of the user. Examples are a morning view, a data exploration view and a coding view. The agent changes the arrangement while the user works.

Agents are the motivation, not a requirement. The same scene can host a pixel-perfect Windows XP desktop, a keyboard-driven tiling setup or a KDE-like workflow. It can also host a kind of human-machine interaction that does not exist yet. Chora ships none of them. Chora makes all of them possible.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
1. Everything is a plugin. The core has no policy: no layout, no focus model, no keybindings, no decorations, no defaults. The window manager is a plugin too. A core without plugins shows a black screen.
  2. Safety is the only built-in behavior. The core keeps an escape hatch that no plugin can override: VT switch, quit, and an emergency reset. Agents will write broken code live, so this exception is necessary.
  3. Lean core, fast stability. A small core reaches feature completeness fast. Then the project hardens it. Features grow in plugins, not in the core.
  4. Reuse before writing. Wayland protocol handling, rendering, widgets, shells and services already exist. Chora connects these parts and writes only what is missing. Fixes go upstream. Every decision gets a check for existing alternatives.
  5. One API for every caller. Plugins, scripts, the CLI, services and agents use the same scene language. An agent can change everything that a user can configure, and it can change it live.
  6. Live and real time. Changes apply while the session runs. They need no restart and cause no noticeable latency.
  7. Declarative and versioned. The configuration is plain text in git: views in YAML, and flavors as bundles of files. A diff shows each change. An agent can read and write the files easily.
  8. Isolation by default. Plugins run as separate processes, services in containers. Input injection and screen capture need the approval of the user.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Start as an experimentation platform. Reach a stable, feature-complete core fast, then start testing.
  • Run as an additional session on a Fedora host, next to the existing desktops. The concrete host is a derived secureblue image.
  • Add features as plugins and as services in containers.
  • Let a coordinator install and connect plugins and services. The first coordinator is the user. A later coordinator is an agent with special permissions that can also write new plugins and services.
  • Make it possible to rebuild any existing workflow, with effort, and to invent new ones.

docs.title: Non-goals for now
docs.text:
• A usable desktop out of the box. A flavor can supply one. The core never does.
  • Agent memory and a local inventory of reusable elements. These form a separate, opinionated layer on top of Chora (see Idea backlog).
  • Distributions other than Fedora and secureblue, and GPUs other than AMD and Intel, until the core is stable.
